cues.text: Let's turn to quality assurance as a team activity, and to what happens when things go wrong: defects.
The first idea is that QA is everyone's responsibility.
Quality is not something one department sprinkles on at the end.
Each role contributes in its own way.
Developers unit test their own code and review each other's work.
Testers design risk-based test cases, meaning they put the most testing effort where failure would be most likely or most damaging.
Product owners validate the acceptance criteria, confirming that what was built meets the conditions the business agreed to.
Operations checks deployability and monitoring: can this software be released safely, and can we see how it behaves once it is live?
Two terms describe when quality work happens.
Shift-left means integrating quality early, so that checking starts near the beginning of the lifecycle rather than at the end.
Shift-right is the opposite end: monitoring actual production behaviour, but with safe controls, so that observing real use does not itself put users or data at risk.
Early checking and live observation work together.
Several practices support prevention, which means stopping defects from being introduced in the first place.
The source lists them: code review, static checks, continuous integration, traceability, test plans, peer review and retrospectives.
Code review and peer review put a second pair of eyes on the work.
Static checks analyse code without running it.
Continuous integration merges and checks changes frequently.
Traceability links requirements to the design, code and tests that cover them.
Test plans set out in advance what will be tested and how.
Retrospectives let the team look back and improve its process.
Now the defect lifecycle, in order.
A defect is first reported.
Then it is triaged, which means assessed and sorted.
Next it is assigned to someone, who investigates it.
After investigation comes the fix, followed by retesting.
Finally the defect is either closed, if the fix works, or reopened, if it does not.
When you record a defect, capture these things: severity, which measures impact; priority, which measures urgency; the environment; the steps to reproduce; evidence; and the owner.
Keep severity and priority distinct.
Severity asks how much damage the defect does.
Priority asks how soon it must be dealt with.
Consider this example.
A runtime crash that happens under valid large uploads or poor network conditions is a failure.
The system did not behave as it should even though the user did nothing wrong.
How severe it is depends on the harm it causes.
Finally, watch for reopened critical bugs.
The source says they suggest one of three problems: insufficient fix validation, an environment mismatch, or poor closure criteria.
In other words, the fix was not properly checked, or it was checked somewhere that differs from where the bug occurred, or the team had no clear standard for when a defect counts as closed.
Next is root cause analysis.
Techniques include the 5 Whys, the fishbone diagram, and the gathering of evidence.
The 5 Whys means asking why repeatedly until you reach the underlying cause.
A fishbone diagram organises possible causes into branches.
The aim is to find the underlying cause, not to assign blame.
Here is the source's example.
Suppose duplicate charges keep recurring.
Patching only the user interface treats a symptom.
Instead, examine idempotency, which is whether repeating the same operation produces the same result as doing it once.
Examine retries, transaction boundaries, and missing tests.
Then fix the systemic cause and add regression tests, which are tests that confirm the problem does not return.
Last, quality metrics.
The source names six: escaped defects, defect density measured as defects per KLOC, pass rate, reopen rate, coverage, and time to resolve.
Escaped defects are those that got through to production.
Defect density is the number of defects per KLOC.
Pass rate is how many tests pass.
Reopen rate is how often closed defects return.
Coverage is how much is exercised by tests.
Time to resolve is how long defects take to fix.
One warning applies to all of them: never treat any single metric as proof in isolation.
Each is a signal that needs context and should be read alongside the others.
